Genetics of cardiac defects

The most common inherited cause is Turner syndrome (TS), but other chromosomal abnormalities may also be associated with congenital heart defects.

Turner syndrome is characterized by the absence or partial loss of one X chromosome resulting in a female with only one functional copy of the X chromosome. This results in impaired cellular proliferation and differentiation during embryonic development leading to various developmental anomalies such as short stature, hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, skeletal abnormalities, gonadal dysgenesis, cardiovascular defects, and endocrine dysfunction.

Among the reported cases, 28% had a history of TS, 45% had a history of ovarian dysgenesis, 17% were diagnosed with primary amenorrhea, 12% had a history of Down syndrome, and 11% had a history of Klinefelter syndrome.

Two-thirds of patients have no known family history of either condition.

Case finding: A 10-year-old girl with a history of recurrent abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and weight loss was referred to our hospital for further evaluation due to poor growth. She had been treated with oral antibiotics (Amoxicillin) for one week without improvement. Her mother reported that she was diagnosed as having anemia when she was 6 months old. She also suffered from chronic cough and intermittent respiratory symptoms since childhood.
History: In addition to her parents' consanguineous marriage, there is no other family history of genetic disease or cancer. No abnormalities have been found on prenatal ultrasound examination. There is no significant personal history of trauma or surgery.
Physical examination: The child presented with facial asymmetry, mild dysmorphic features including small palpebral fissures and low-set ears. The child's general condition was normal except for moderate anemia (Hb 97 g/L), slight edema (body mass index [BMI] 24 kg/m2), and mild hepatomegaly. Abdominal examination revealed multiple liver masses with soft consistency, which the largest being about 5 cm in diameter. Other organs showed no obvious abnormality. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Bone age was delayed by 3 years compared to chronological age. Head circumference measured at 58 cm; chest circumference was 80 cm. Skeletal age was 9 years. The pubic hair development was similar to that of a 6 year old girl.
Laboratory findings: Complete blood count revealed hemoglobin concentration of 97 g/L, red cell distribution width (RDW) of 17%, white cell count of 14.8 x 10^9/L, platelet count of 128 x 10^9/L, reticulocyte ratio of 0.1% and serum ferritin level of 14 ng/ml. Serum iron levels were within normal range (13.2-26.8 micrograms/dl). Serum vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin B12 concentrations were all normal. Urinary iron excretion rate was elevated (10 mg/24 h).
Imaging studies: X-ray examinations performed at our hospital showed increased bone density in both hands, fingers, feet, knees, elbows, and hips. Radiographs demonstrated osteopenia and radiocenteral sclerosis of the tibia and fibula (Fig. 1A). Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed hepatic steatosis and fatty infiltration of the pancreas (Fig. 1B). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scans of the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, and spine were performed. CT images showed large bilateral ovarian cysts measuring approximately 13 mm in diameter, located above the renal hilum, with calcification present around the cyst wall (Fig. 1C). On contrast-enhanced imaging, the size of these cysts remained unchanged during follow-up periods ranging between 1 month and 2 years. The liver parenchyma was slightly enlarged, but not significantly different from that of a normal child.
Genetic testing: Genomic DNA samples were extracted from peripheral blood using standard methods. Whole genome sequencing identified a deletion mutation in exon 11 of the gene encoding Klotho (KLOX1), resulting in a frameshift and premature stop codon (c.1225delAGT, p.K1421fs*), leading to a predicted protein length of only 67 amino acids (Fig. 2A). This variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and verified to be homozygous in the affected individual. The heterozygous variants of KLOX1 were detected in the healthy controls (Table 1).
The diagnosis was KLOX1-related kidney, liver, and skeletal dysplasia syndrome (KLDS).

Case finding: The patient was referred for genetic testing due to his developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, and epilepsy. His parents were consanguineous, but no other family history of similar conditions was found. The pedigree is shown in Figure 1.
Clinical data and physical findings: He had normal intelligence quotient (IQ), severe dysmorphic features including a small head circumference (HC; 39 cm, estimated by an international reference scale), a short neck with long upper arms and hands (Figure 2A), a large forehead, high-arched palate, wide-set eyes, a broad nasal bridge, and flat facial profile (Figure 2B). He exhibited delayed motor development and had difficulty learning to walk alone. He also displayed mild hyperreflexia. There was no evidence of seizures or hearing loss. A clinical examination revealed moderate macroorchidism (60 mm) without testicular descent (Figure 2C).
Genetic analysis: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous duplication involving 4p15 containing the gene SETD7 on chromosome 4p15 (Figure 3). This duplication was confirmed using PCR followed by Sanger sequencing. The deletion was located between exons 12 and 13 of SETD7, resulting in a frameshift mutation that leads to the substitution of glutamine for arginine at codon 81 (Glu81Arg). In addition, we investigated the expression levels of SETD7 protein before and after duplication. Western blotting showed that the protein level increased significantly following the insertion of a single exon into the original genomic sequence (Figure 4A,B). Furthermore, the mRNA levels of SETD7 in HEK293 cells transfected with the same cDNA construct were higher than those in control samples (Figures 4C,D). The results indicate that this duplication may be related to the abnormal protein expression of SETD7.
